Thanks for your positive feedback and your interest in our work. We are very pleased about your question and would like to give a more detailed answer to that.  

In general, the challenge with radar-based perception is very different from LiDAR- or camera-based perception. The main challenge for LiDAR- or camera-based perception is the efficient retrieval of information to make good decisions, whereas the challenge for radar-based perception is the effective retrieval of information. This does not mean that radar-based perception does not have to be efficient or vice versa, but the main focus of radar-based perception is the retrieval of as much information as possible from very little (sparse and noisy) input data. In contrast, LiDAR- or camera-based perception has to efficiently retrieve information from the vast amount of given input data. Therefore, the focus within these two domains is very different (as long as we are not considering low-level radar data). As a consequence, Graph Neural Networks (or Transformers as a subset of attentional GNNs) seem to be a suitable choice since they cannot just use the information of the radar points themselves but also the information of the relationships between the points. However, this comes at the cost of a preliminary graph construction (or the computational complexity of O(N²) for the Transformer variant). Nevertheless, for a low number of input points, this is a valid model choice.

The architectural question aside, the analysis of the RadarGNN model reveals multiple issues that can be addressed. The model  

1.	fails to detect VRUs and small objects,  
2.	performs worse in the terminal environment and,  
3.	struggles to accurately predict object orientations.   

The inability of the model to detect VRUs and small objects can be subject to multiple route causes. First, VRUs are characterized by a low radar reflectivity (~0dBm²) and are therefore represented by a low number of radar points, similar to small objects, which makes them inherently difficult to detect. To overcome this problem, one could aggregate multiple radar sweeps to create a denser radar point cloud (which is already done by RadarGNN) but has to consider motion blurring. Besides that, RadarGNN uses a quite simple network architecture with only five consecutive GNN layers and consistent spatial dimensions. However, spatial encoding (and decoding) has been proven very effective in extracting essential information and reducing noise. Moreover, this would allow the usage of multi-level feature maps to detect objects of different sizes. However, an encoder-decoder architecture comes at the cost of calculating multiple graphs and is, therefore, computationally expensive. In addition to an improved feature extractor, multiple detection heads could be added to allow task specialization. Last but not least, data augmentation (especially object sampling) could be used to improve the detection performance for the minority classes. In summary, data, model, and training-based methods can be used to improve the model’s performance in detecting VRUs and small objects.  
 
To improve the model performance in terminal environments, the input noise and multipath reflections have to be reduced. Therefore, conventional or learnable filters can be used, which includes the aforementioned autoencoders. An oversampling of the terminal scenes could also improve the model's performance.

The prediction of object orientations could be improved by creating a continuous output space by splitting the angle into its sine and cosine components or converting the regression problem into a classification problem by splitting the heading angle into multiple sectors [30]. Data augmentation could also be an option since we are only using the translational equivariant version of the RadarGNN model and not the SE(2) invariant bounding box encoding.

In summary, there are a multitude of different possibilities to improve the performance of RadarGNN and similar radar-based perception methods. In general, 3D object detection for 4D radar sensors is still a major research gap, and especially, the availability of open-source algorithms is very limited. To address this, we are providing 4D radar data in our TruckScenes dataset and hoping to accelerate research in the field of radar-based perception and sensor fusion.

```
[30] Zhou, Yi, et al. "On the continuity of rotation representations in neural networks." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2019.
```

We would like to express our sincere appreciation to the reviewers for taking the time to provide such thorough feedback. We are very pleased with the reviewer's comments describing our work as “significant to the research community” and “a significant milestone in autonomous driving research”. We have been working hard to tackle the reviewer's suggestions and further improve the quality of our submission. We'd be very grateful for any further feedback and will promptly address any such inputs to the best of our ability.

> If possible, please provide more annotation types after the release, for example, the point-level semantics annotations.  

We share the assessment for the need for more detailed annotations and are already discussing different extensions of the current dataset. In this context, we are taking map-based extensions as well as semantic labels into account but have to consider the high costs of point-level semantic annotations. Nevertheless, we welcome any suggestions for future data set extensions and are very grateful for any feedback from the community.

> The related work part seems a little bit, overlooking other datasets, e.g., K-Radar, view-of-delft, for autonomous driving. Please incresea the converage of the literature review and introduce some related works in algorithm if possible.  

We admit that the related work section is somewhat limited due to space limitations. However, we agree that the inclusion of closely related datasets like the aiMotive [22], K-Radar [23], or View-of-Delft [24] would be beneficial for the reader. > Although as a dataset paper, the experiments part of this work are expected to be more richful. Only one old baseline method, CenterPoint, with lidar point cloud as input, was evaluated on the dataset. The users might want to see the comparison between different modalities in the object detection and tracking tasks. Moreover, it is better to provide some qualitative results in the rain and fog weather, which can help the users to understand the performance and usability of this dataset.  

We agree that the provision of more baseline models is valuable to the users of the dataset, and we have been working hard to provide a broader selection of comparison models. Thus, we will include a baseline model for every modality (LiDAR, radar, camera) and also work on baseline models for sensor fusion applications. The following table shows the preliminary results of two additional baseline models for the camera and radar domain in comparison to the CenterPoint LiDAR model.

| Method           | Modality | NDS  | mAP  | ATE  | ASE  | AOE  | AVE  | AAE  |
|------------------|----------|------|------|------|------|------|------|------|
| PETR [25]        | Camera   | 0.10 | 0.02 | 1.07 | 0.73 | 0.73 | 1.62 | 0.62 |
| RadarGNN [26]    | Radar    | 0.11 | 0.07 | 0.89 | 0.81 | 1.13 | 8.00 | 0.57 |
| CenterPoint [17] | LiDAR    | 0.43 | 0.30 | 0.40 | 0.35 | 0.29 | 2.93 | 0.20 |

We will also include an analysis of their performance and qualitative results in the appendix to create a better understanding of the performance and help with the usability of the dataset. As a summary of our first analysis, we can already say that the higher radar point cloud density leads to higher performance compared to nuScenes (0.11 NDS on TruckScenes vs. 0.06 NDS on nuScenes). Nevertheless, detecting VRUs or correctly estimating the orientation of the objects remains challenging for radar-only object detection. Moreover, the terminal environment represents a major challenge because of the high number of metal shipping containers, which leads to multipath reflections and noise in the radar data. Besides that, we observed that the PETR camera model cannot be easily transferred to the TruckScenes dataset and has significant problems with its high detection range. Therefore, we will investigate different camera models to create a robust baseline to compare to.
In addition, we are working on the inclusion of more modern baselines like Voxel Mamba [27] for the LiDAR or Sparse4D [28] for the camera domain and currently training BEVFusion [29] to provide baseline results for sensor fusion applications. Furthermore, we will constantly extend the baseline results for different perception tasks. Thus, we have already planned a tracking and prediction task and the provision of corresponding baseline results.

> From the story aspect, it is better to emphasize the advantages of sensing robustness of 4D radar under adverse weathers. This helps to augment the necessity of providing 4d radar data and collecting driving data from adverse weathers.  

We thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestion and will adjust our argumentation such that logistics has to remain operational under all conditions, which is why robust perception is even more important for autonomous trucking. 

> Better to provide the picture of the real truck used for data collection, with the sensor suite exhbited clearly.

A picture of the real truck with its sensor suite and videos of the recording drives will be shown on our website. In addition, we will include an image of the real truck in the appendix of the paper.

We truly appreciate the reviewer's time and thoughtful feedback on our manuscript. We are honored that the reviewer highlighted the high significance of this work and described our dataset as “meticulously curated”, which “fills a critical gap in autonomous vehicle datasets”. In the following, we will respond to the reviewer’s feedback and update our manuscript accordingly. Please let us know if any of our responses are unclear or if a new question arose. We will do our best to clarify any ambiguities and further comments.  

> The dataset is collected primarily in Germany, which might limit its applicability to other regions with different road conditions and traffic behaviours. It is worth expanding to a new, structurally different roads like in the UK. […] The dataset is recorded from a single autonomous test truck, which might limit the diversity of the sensor perspectives and configurations.  

We fully agree with the reviewer that expanding the dataset to new, structurally different roads, countries, and multiple test vehicles with different sensor perspectives would be beneficial to enhance the dataset’s applicability and remove potential biases. In this regard, we are already in contact with our partners to discuss the possibilities of a European truck dataset with multiple test vehicles, but considering the high costs and legislation efforts of such an undertaking, this would have to remain future work for now.  

> Despite the rigorous quality assurance process, manual annotations are inherently prone to errors. Future work could explore semi-automated or fully automated annotation methods as well as automatic validation (e.g. neurosymbolic AI) to improve consistency.  

We thank the reviewer for recommending Neuro-symbolic AI methods for automatic validation since we have not considered those methods yet. Currently, we are already using over 200 different automated tests to ensure high data quality and over 20 different tests to check the annotation quality. Nevertheless, we are constantly improving our pipeline and working closely with our quality assurance partner to enhance the annotation quality and label consistency even further.  

> The discussion on the potential negative societal impact is somewhat limited. While the dataset adheres to GDPR directives, a deeper exploration of ethical considerations, such as the impact of autonomous trucking on employment and safety concerns, would be beneficial.  

We admit that the discussion of potential societal impacts is somewhat limited in the submitted manuscript. To address this, we will include findings on possible changes in society, employment, and sustainability [19 - 21], provide a deeper exploration of ethical considerations [21], and discuss safety concerns of autonomous trucking [21].  

```
[19] Escherle, Svenja, Emilia Darlagiannis, and Anna Sprung. "Automated trucks and the future of logistics: A Delphi-based scenario study." Logistics Research 16.1 (2023): 1-21.  
[20] Escherle, Svenja, Anna Sprung, and Klaus Bengler. "How Will Automated Trucks Change the Processes and Roles in Hub-to-Hub Transport?." International Conference on Human-Computer Interaction. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2023.
```

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper presents "MAN TruckScenes," the first large-scale multimodal dataset specifically designed for autonomous trucking. This dataset aims to address the unique challenges faced by autonomous trucks, such as trailer occlusions, novel sensor perspectives, and terminal environments. It includes over 740 scenes of 20 seconds each, collected in various environmental conditions using a comprehensive sensor suite: 4 cameras, 6 lidar, 6 radar sensors, 2 IMUs, and a high-precision GNSS. The dataset features manually annotated 3D bounding boxes for 27 object classes and 15 attributes, and it is the first to provide 4D radar data with 360° coverage. Additionally, it includes extensive dataset analysis and baseline results.

review.value:
The dataset is meticulously curated, ensuring high-quality annotations through a multi-stage labelling and quality assurance process. The comprehensive sensor suite and the large number of annotated scenes make it a valuable resource for developing and testing perception algorithms for autonomous trucks.

The paper is well-written and provides a detailed description of the dataset, including sensor specifications, synchronization, calibration, data processing, and annotation procedures. The inclusion of figures and tables aids in understanding the dataset's scope and quality.

The originality of the work lies in its focus on autonomous trucking, a domain with unique challenges not adequately addressed by existing datasets. The inclusion of 4D radar data and the focus on long-range detection further enhance its novelty.

The significance of this work is high, as it fills a critical gap in autonomous vehicle datasets by providing data specific to heavy-duty trucks. This can significantly accelerate the development of perception systems for autonomous trucking, which has substantial implications for logistics and transportation safety.

strengths.value: Significant Contribution: The dataset addresses a crucial gap in autonomous vehicle research, providing data specific to the unique challenges of autonomous trucks. High-Quality Data: The multi-stage annotation and quality assurance process ensures high-quality annotations, crucial for training reliable models. Comprehensive Sensor Suite: The dataset includes data from a wide range of sensors, offering a rich multimodal resource for perception research. Diverse Environmental Conditions: The data is collected in various weather conditions, times of day, and different geographic locations, enhancing its robustness. Innovative Use of 4D Radar: The inclusion of 4D radar data with 360° coverage is a significant innovation, offering valuable data for developing advanced perception algorithms.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: Geographical Limitation: The dataset is collected primarily in Germany, which might limit its applicability to other regions with different road conditions and traffic behaviours. It is worth expanding to a new, structurally different roads like in the UK. Single Vehicle Data: The dataset is recorded from a single autonomous test truck, which might limit the diversity of the sensor perspectives and configurations. Annotation Challenges: Despite the rigorous quality assurance process, manual annotations are inherently prone to errors. Future work could explore semi-automated or fully automated annotation methods as well as automatic validation (e.g. neurosymbolic AI) to improve consistency.

limitations.value: The authors have adequately addressed the limitations of their work, including the geographical limitation to Germany and the use of a single autonomous test truck. They also discuss the potential inaccuracies in annotations despite the extensive quality assurance process. However, the discussion on the potential negative societal impact is somewhat limited. While the dataset adheres to GDPR directives, a deeper exploration of ethical considerations, such as the impact of autonomous trucking on employment and safety concerns, would be beneficial.

correctness.value: The claims made in the submission appear to be correct. The detailed description of the dataset creation, including sensor synchronization, calibration, and data processing, is thorough and convincing. The provided baseline results and dataset analysis further support the validity of the dataset.

clarity.value: The paper is well-organized and clearly written. The use of figures, tables, and detailed explanations enhances its readability and comprehension. The structure follows a logical flow, from the introduction of the problem to the detailed description of the dataset and its potential applications.

relation_to_prior_work.value: The paper provides a comprehensive review of existing autonomous driving datasets and clearly distinguishes the unique contributions of MAN TruckScenes. It effectively highlights the gaps in existing datasets and explains how the new dataset addresses these gaps.

documentation.value: Authors confirmed that they will provide documentation with detailed information on sensor setup, data collection, synchronization, calibration, and annotation. The authors also provide a development kit, evaluation code, and detailed annotation instructions, ensuring transparency and reproducibility. The dataset is published under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license, promoting open research while protecting the data.

title.value: The first multimodal dataset for autonomous trucking.

summary_and_contributions.value: The authors have released a multimodal dataset containing 740 scenes, each 20 seconds long, recorded under various environmental conditions. This dataset is specifically tailored for autonomous trucking, addressing unique challenges such as trailer occlusion and novel sensor perspectives. The manually annotated ground truth includes temporally consistent 3D bounding boxes up to 230 meters, enabling models designed for long-range detection. Additionally, the dataset features 4D radar with 360-degree coverage, making it the largest radar dataset for 3D object detection.

review.value:
Autonomous trucking is one of the most promising areas poised for transformation by autonomous driving technology. Despite this potential, there has been no publicly available dataset specifically designed for autonomous trucking. The authors have released MAN TruckScenes, the first large-scale dataset to address this gap.

This dataset includes scenarios recorded across different seasons, times of day, and weather conditions, and covers a wide geographical area. Additionally, it features logistic terminals among the recorded scenarios. The dataset description is thorough, providing relevant details such as sensor setup, synchronization, calibration, and scene selection framed as an optimization problem.

From my first-hand experience, I have observed how models trained on personal vehicle data perform when applied to data recorded by trucks. The motivation for this dataset is clearly articulated, and the need for a dedicated autonomous trucking dataset is well-founded.

However, the dataset's primary limitation is that it was recorded exclusively in one country, where trucks are required to use the rightmost lane whenever possible. This could introduce a bias in the data distribution, potentially hindering the generalization ability of models trained on this dataset.

Strengths & Limitations:
See the corresponding sections

strengths.value:
- A 3D object detection dataset tailored to autonomous trucking.
- Very high-quality dataset documentation.
- A large amount of 4D radar data.
- Annotations up to 230 meters.
- nuScenes format for ensuring easy integration.
- Since debris is included among the categories, the dataset can be used for general obstacle detection tasks.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: Expand the data collection area to alleviate the issue of rightmost-lane driving.

limitations.value: The authors mentioned the limitations of the proposed dataset (recording in one country with one test truck, and calibration issues). Additional limitations are described in the appendix (rightmost lane trucking).

correctness.value: The dataset was constructed soundly, taking into account diversity using an optimization method. The dataset documentation contains information regarding data collection, maintenance, annotation guidelines, etc.

clarity.value: The paper is well-written and easy to follow.

relation_to_prior_work.value: The authors have provided an adequate amount of related work. However, I would suggest including the aiMotive dataset (Matuszka, Tamas, et al. "aiMotive Dataset: A Multimodal Dataset for Robust Autonomous Driving with Long-Range Perception." International Conference on Learning Representations 2023 Workshop on Scene Representations for Autonomous Driving). This dataset is likely the most closely related due to its multimodal nature, and the inclusion of numerous highway scenes, tunnel passages, and long-range annotations.

documentation.value: The supplementary material includes detailed documentation in Data Cards Playbook format, sensor specification and annotation guidelines, and code for reproducibility. The documentation is high-quality and contains all the required information.

ethics.value: I did not find any ethical concerns.

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value: Please let the reviewers know when the full dataset is available.

title.value: This dataset is significant to the research community but needs further efforts to improve its presentation, experiments and content.

summary_and_contributions.value: This work presents the first multimodal dataset for autonomous trucking, allowing the research community to address truck-specific challenges. This dataset features in its richful scenes, redundant sensor equipment and high-quality annotations. The dataset is organized in the same way as nuScenes to ensure compatibility and can support many perception tasks.

review.value:
1. This dataset is significant to the research community. It includes six 4D radar sensors with a spatial coverage of nearly 360 degrees, enabling the research in surrounding perception algorithms development. Moreover, the dataset is collected in the context of autonomous trucking, inducing new research problems from the platform aspect. 
2. This paper is well-organized and presented clearly. Many collection and implementation details are provided for reference. 
3. Although as a dataset paper, the experiments part of this work are expected to be more richful. Only one old baseline method, CenterPoint, with lidar point cloud as input, was evaluated on the dataset. The users might want to see the comparison between different modalities in the object detection and tracking tasks. Moreover, it is better to provide some qualitative results in the rain and fog weather, which can help the users to understand the performance and usability of this dataset. 
4. The annotations of this dataset is enough to support most autonomous driving perception tasks, except for the semantic segmentation, semantic completion task. It’s good to see the authors providing such annotations in the future. 
5. The related work part seems a little bit, overlooking other datasets, e.g., K-Radar, view-of-delft, for autonomous driving. Please incresea the converage of the literature review and introduce some related works in algorithm if possible.

strengths.value: This contribution fills the niche of autonomous trucking dataset, being a significant milestone in autonomous driving research. The whole community could benefit from the dataset, not only by using their data collected from truck applications, but also by using the surrounding 4D radar data. The presentation is also good and much details are provided in the supplementary materials.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: From the story aspect, it is better to emphasize the advantages of sensing robustness of 4D radar under adverse weathers. This helps to augment the necessity of providing 4d radar data and collecting driving data from adverse weathers. If possible, please provide more annotation types after the release, for example, the point-level semantics annotations. Better to use the ‘LiDAR’ term instead of lidar. The experiments part needs to be improved by comparing more modalities and baseline methods. Qualitative results are important for the dataset contribution.

limitations.value: Yes, the authors did anonymization for the image data as a data protection measures.

correctness.value: Yes, the claims are consistent with the real contribution and the dataset is constructed in a sound way.

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value: Better to provide the picture of the real truck used for data collection, with the sensor suite exhbited clearly.

title.value: MAN TruckScenes: A multimodal dataset for autonomous trucking in diverse conditions

TLDR.value: The first multimodal dataset for autonomous trucking

abstract.value: Autonomous trucking is a promising technology that can greatly impact modern logistics and the environment. Ensuring its safety on public roads is one of the main duties that requires an accurate perception of the environment. To achieve this, machine learning methods rely on large datasets, but to this day, no such datasets are available for autonomous trucks. In this work, we present MAN TruckScenes, the first multimodal dataset for autonomous trucking. MAN TruckScenes allows the research community to come into contact with truck-specific challenges, such as trailer occlusions, novel sensor perspectives, and terminal environments for the first time. It comprises more than 740 scenes of 20 s each within a multitude of different environmental conditions. The sensor set includes 4 cameras, 6 lidar, 6 radar sensors, 2 IMUs, and a high-precision GNSS. The dataset's 3D bounding boxes were manually annotated and carefully reviewed to achieve a high quality standard. Bounding boxes are available for 27 object classes, 15 attributes, and a range of more than 230 m. The scenes are tagged according to 34 distinct scene tags, and all objects are tracked throughout the scene to promote a wide range of applications. Additionally, MAN TruckScenes is the first dataset to provide 4D radar data with 360° coverage and is thereby the largest radar dataset with annotated 3D bounding boxes. Finally, we provide extensive dataset analysis and baseline results. The dataset, development kit, and more will be available online.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
